'''Johann Friedrich Bonhoeffer''' (August 10, 1932 – January 29, 2021), more often '''Friedrich Bonhoeffer''', was a German neuroscientist and physicist known for pioneering studies in [[axon guidance]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Baier |first=Herwig |date=2021-04-21 |title=Friedrich Bonhoeffer (1932–2021) |journal=Neuron |language=English |volume=109 |issue=8 |pages=1255–1257 |doi=10.1016/j.neuron.2021.04.003 |issn=0896-6273 |pmid=33887192|s2cid=233328883 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=Dev>{{Cite journal |last=Drescher |first=Uwe |title=Obituary: Friedrich Bonhoeffer (1932-2021) |journal=Development |year=2021 |volume=148 |issue=4 |article-number=dev199522 |doi=10.1242/dev.199522|s2cid=232056270 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Klein |first1=Rüdiger |last2=Wilkinson |first2=David |last3=Herrera |first3=Eloisa |date=2022 |title=Editorial – Friedrich Bonhoeffer (1932–2021) |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0306452222005759 |journal=Neuroscience |volume=508 |language=en |pages=S0306452222005759 |doi=10.1016/j.neuroscience.2022.11.019|pmid=36427670 |s2cid=253835531 |hdl=10261/307551 |hdl-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Education and career ==
{{more sources|section|date=October 2025}}
Bonhoeffer was born in [[Frankfurt]], Germany. He was the grandson of noted psychiatrist [[Karl Bonhoeffer]] and the son of physical chemist [[Karl-Friedrich Bonhoeffer]]. From a young age, Bonhoeffer was interested in physics and chemistry, and went on to study physics at the [[University of Göttingen]], where he received his PhD in [[nuclear physics]] in 1958 under the supervision of [[Arnold Flammersfeld]]. After his doctoral studies, Bonhoeffer was inspired by a lecture by [[Max Delbrück]] to switch from studying [[neutrino]]s to [[nucleic acid]]s. He received a [[Fulbright scholarship]] and went to the United States to do postdoctoral research in the lab of [[Howard Schachman]] at the [[University of California, Berkeley]]. In 1960, he returned to Germany to work with [[Alfred Gierer]] at the Max Planck Institute for Virus Research. He soon became the director of the institute, where he began researching axon guidance, the process by which axons of neurons grow and branch out to find their targets in the developing nervous system.

Throughout the 1970s and 1980s, Bonhoeffer made a series of landmark contributions to understanding the molecular mechanisms behind axon guidance. He developed key techniques that are still widely used today, and used them to uncover fundamental axon guidance mechanisms. His discoveries led to the identification of the first known [[Ephrin]] guidance molecules, as well as other [[axon guidance]] mechanisms.<ref name=Dev /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Friedrich Bonhoeffer {{!}} Gruber Foundation |url=https://gruber.yale.edu/friedrich-bonhoeffer |access-date=2022-12-15 |website=gruber.yale.edu}}</ref>

In 1984, Bonhoeffer became the director of the newly founded [[Max Planck Institute for Developmental Biology]], a position he held until his retirement in 2000. He continued to be involved with the institute as an emeritus director.

== Honors and awards ==
Bonhoeffer's work has been recognized with numerous awards and honors, including memberships in the [[German academy of sciences leopoldina|German Academy of Sciences, Leopoldina]], and the [[European Molecular Biology Organization]]. He was a co-recipient of the [[Gruber Prize in Neuroscience]] in 2020.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2020 Gruber Neuroscience Prize {{!}} Gruber Foundation |url=https://gruber.yale.edu/prize/2020-gruber-neuroscience-prize |access-date=2025-10-15 |website=gruber.yale.edu}}</ref>
== Miscellaneous ==
The sea snail species ''[[Lophiotoma friedrichbonhoefferi]]'', discovered by his colleague and friend [[Baldomero Olivera]], bears his name.<ref name="WoRMS">{{WRMS species|389134|''Lophiotoma friedrichbonhoefferi'' Olivera, 2004||5 April 2010}}</ref>
